# SK7100 — The documentation duplicates the base member's

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A member's documentation comment is word for word the one on the member it overrides or implements, so `<inheritdoc />` says the same thing and cannot fall out of step with it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Maintainability |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| ReSharper | `InheritdocConsiderUsage` (`resharper_inheritdoc_consider_usage_highlighting`) |

## Why

A copied doc comment is accurate on the day it is written and has no mechanism keeping it so. The base member's prose is the one a reader treats as authoritative, and when it is edited the copy below silently starts describing the previous behaviour — which is worse than no documentation, because a reader has no way to tell which of the two is stale. `<inheritdoc />` cannot drift, because there is nothing for it to drift from: it is a reference rather than a copy, and it is exactly as long as the claim it makes.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
public abstract class Store {
    /// <summary>Removes every entry.</summary>
    public abstract void Clear();
}

public sealed class MemoryStore : Store {
    /// <summary>Removes every entry.</summary>
    public override void Clear() { }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
public abstract class Store {
    /// <summary>Removes every entry.</summary>
    public abstract void Clear();
}

public sealed class MemoryStore : Store {
    /// <inheritdoc />
    public override void Clear() { }
}
```

## The ReSharper mapping

⚠ The export sets `resharper_inheritdoc_consider_usage_highlighting = none` and this rule defaults to `suggestion`. Reading the ReSharper key — off by default, doc 03 § "Severities" — switches it off. The difference is deliberate rather than an oversight: this rule fires only where the two comments are *identical*, which ReSharper's inspection does not require, so the finding it produces is narrower and does not need the low severity that keeps the wider one usable. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Identical, not similar, and there is deliberately no threshold.** The two comments are compared as their text with the `///` markers stripped and runs of whitespace collapsed, ordinally. A word changed, an `<exception>` added, a `<param>` the base does not carry — any of those is prose saying something the base does not, and replacing it with `<inheritdoc />` would delete it. A similarity score is what would make this rule dangerous, so it does not have one. ⚠ **Three ways to have a base member, all covered, and ambiguity is silence.** An `override`, an explicit interface implementation and an implicit one all resolve; a member that implements *two* interface members resolves to nothing, because `<inheritdoc />` would have to pick one and picking is not a mechanical edit. ⚠ **A member documented in more than one block is left alone**, because the fix replaces a span and an ordinary comment sitting between two documentation blocks would be deleted with them. ⚠ **A base in metadata is compared through its XML documentation file**, and a referenced assembly shipped without one answers with nothing — which is silence, not a match. ⚠ **The one real behaviour change is downstream of the compiler.** `csc` writes `<inheritdoc />` into the generated XML documentation file literally rather than expanding it, so a consumer that reads that file without resolving inheritdoc sees a member with no prose. Every current documentation generator and the IDE do resolve it; a bespoke XML post-processor may not, and that is the case to check before turning this on. It is why the rule ships at `suggestion` rather than `warning`.
